title: Nola
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: Hyman notes that Yuchasin lists this expression with reference to [Bava Metzia 67a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Metzia.67a.5-6).
Seder HaDorot discusses it at length. Hyman explains that it is an Aramaic expression, not a sage’s name. When someone wants to say “I and he” or “I and she,” they say “I and nola.”[^3]

notes.text: The works abbreviated כ״מ and כ״הד and the exact wording of the final Aramaic expression remain unresolved. The English does not admit a new sage named Nola.

Supplied מכ״מ סו. and כ״הד remain unresolved work labels; the מ prefix is a contextual from, not a proved acronym registry entry. סו. is shown literally beside the conventional66a interpretation, since the work and pagination are unidentified. Earlier BavaMetzia66a and Rif nonmatches are finite inherited reports, not fresh universal absence. A Bach-on-Rif search lead is not a checked Yuchasin witness. Hyman’s negative not a sage’s name and his I-and-he/I-and-she explanation are preserved as his account, without declaring the literal אני ונולא corrupt or admitting a new sage.

Hyman’s printed notice (vol. III, p. 920) gives Bava Metzia 67a and Seder HaDorot where the supplied transcription has מכ״מ סו. and בכ״הד. The [1857 London–Edinburgh Yuchasin, p. 171](https://www.daat.ac.il/daat/vl/yohasin-zakut/yohasin-zakut09.pdf#page=27) discusses the expression under ניילא, with נוולא noted as a variant. Zacuto cites the Geonic explanation and rejects reading it as a woman’s name. [Rashi](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Bava_Metzia.67a.5.3) gives both the Geonic explanation and his own suggestion that it is her name. [Shita Mekubetzet](https://www.sefaria.org/Shita_Mekubetzet_on_Bava_Metzia.67a.2) explicitly quotes Rav Tzemach bar Paltoi Gaon’s parallels in Niddah and the Solomon and Ashmedai story. The linked current readings are אנא והוא (“I and he”) at [Niddah 25b](https://www.sefaria.org/Niddah.25b.14) and לחודיה (“alone”) at [Gittin 68b](https://www.sefaria.org/Gittin.68b.14).
